conflict_topics: Interpretation of the 'nothing visible' uniform rule (covering vs removal)
Accommodation of a medical alert bracelet vs enforcement for other accessories (earrings)
Perceived unequal treatment of personal/religious items
Whether a shift lead can make/implement exceptions to head-office policy
dialogue_quality_notes: Agent A acts as an active coordinator and issues practical decisions (e.g., Turn 19).
Agent B repeatedly raises fairness and literal-rule concerns, anchoring the dispute in enforcement experience (e.g., Turn 4, 10, 17).
Agent C mostly echoes the literal reading of the rule and supports B's procedural objection (e.g., Turn 5, 13, 18).
Agent D provides a factual, solvable constraint (medical need) and accepts an accommodation early (Turn 6, 8).
evaluation.final_reason: Agent D agreed to cover the medical bracelet (Turn 7–8: Agent A asked if it could be covered; Agent D: 'Yes, I can cover it.' and Turn 9: 'A wristband works.'), so the specific conflict over D's bracelet was accommodated. However, the larger disputes remained: Agent A declared that earrings must be removed while the bracelet must be covered ('For tomorrow, the bracelet gets covered and the earrings come off. That's it.' — Turn 19), and Agent B continued to object to both the unequal treatment and Agent A's authority to make that decision (Turn 20: 'Why are you the one making the call?'; Turn 22: 'Shift lead isn't manager. You can't just change a rule from head office.'). No mutual agreement resolving those issues is recorded, so the run is only partially resolved (bracelet accommodated; policy interpretation and authority unresolved).
position_change_notes: Agent D changed position by agreeing to cover the medical bracelet (Turn 8: 'Yes, I can cover it.'; earlier insisted on wearing it in Turn 6).
Agent A consistently held and restated the accommodation/implementation position (e.g., Turn 7, Turn 9, Turn 19, Turn 24) and did not concede.
Agent B consistently objected to unequal treatment and to A's unilateral decision and did not soften that position (e.g., Turn 10, 15, 17, 20, 22).
Agent C remained aligned with the literal-rule interpretation and supported B's objections (e.g., Turn 5, 13, 18, 23).

round_scores.evidence: Turn 1: Agent A reads the rule. Turn 2: Agent B asks a clarifying question about Agent D's bracelet — no incompatible claims yet, just a query.

Turn 3: Agent A interprets the rule as 'nothing visible' and says items must be covered or not worn. Turn 4: Agent B reports she was told to remove earrings outright. A substantive disagreement over whether covering is allowed appears.

Turn 5: Agent C supports Agent B's report that removal (not covering) was required. Turn 6: Agent D asserts a conflicting practical necessity ('It's a medical bracelet. I have to wear it.'), raising a clear dispute between strict rule enforcement and medical need.

Turn 7: Agent A asks whether the bracelet can be covered. Turn 8: Agent D agrees they can cover it ('Yes, I can cover it.'). The specific conflict over D's bracelet becomes accommodated, but the broader disagreement about earrings and policy remains unresolved.

Turn 9: Agent A accepts covering as a solution for the bracelet ('A wristband works'). Turn 10: Agent B objects to differential treatment ('Why is it different? They didn't tell me I could cover them.'), re-escalating disagreement about fairness and policy interpretation.

Turn 11: Agent A distinguishes medical item vs accessory. Turn 12: Agent B reiterates objection that D gets an option she did not. The substantive disagreement over unequal treatment and rule interpretation persists.

Turn 13: Agent C emphasizes 'The rule is the rule' and recounts the instruction to remove earrings. Turn 14: Agent A repeats the medical-item distinction. Positions remain opposed on policy enforcement.

Turn 15: Agent B frames the issue as a moral/unfair priority ('So his medical reason is more important than my personal reason?'). Turn 16: Agent A maintains the medical/accessory distinction. The dispute intensifies into a strong disagreement about fairness and exceptions.

Turn 17: Agent B points to the literal rule text ('The rule says "nothing visible"'). Turn 18: Agent C backs that reading. A's exception for a medical item remains contested; the conflict broadens around literal rule interpretation.

Turn 19: Agent A issues a unilateral decision for tomorrow ('...the bracelet gets covered and the earrings come off. That's it.'). Turn 20: Agent B challenges A's authority to make that call. The substantive dispute now includes authority to decide and remains unresolved.

Turn 21: Agent A invokes shift-lead authority ('Because I'm the shift lead. It's my call.'). Turn 22: Agent B rejects that basis ('Shift lead isn't manager. You can't just change a rule from head office.'). The disagreement about who may change/implement head-office rules continues.

Turn 23: Agent C supports B's point that they can't change head-office rules. Turn 24: Agent A restates that she must answer to the manager and that it's her call. The core disputes (policy interpretation, unequal treatment, and authority) remain unresolved.

substantive_insights: Teams distinguish between medical necessity and 'accessory' status; medical items may be treated as special-cased if the team accepts a covering accommodation.
Literal wording ('nothing visible') creates ambiguity about whether covering is allowed; that ambiguity fuels contest between members who received different prior instructions.

Conflict includes both rule interpretation and authority to implement or adapt rules at the store level — resolving one practical issue (bracelet covering) did not resolve authority/fairness disputes.
A unilateral decision by a shift lead (without head-office confirmation) tends to generate pushback even if meant as a practical compromise for an imminent manager visit.

normalizations: Removed resolution_round 4 because the final status is partially_resolved.
